summary: Defines a standard framework for extensible SNMP agents, where subagents handle parts of the management data and a master agent combines them. It is a standards-track document at the draft standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: One front desk person hands your questions to different specialists and returns their answers as one reply.

questions: what is the difference between a master agent and a subagent
how does agentx handle snmp set requests
subtitle: How one SNMP agent can be built from many independent subagents behind a single master agent.

tldr.problem: Managed devices are made of independently installed components, each with its own MIB modules, but the SNMP framework does not say how the set of managed objects an agent supports can change dynamically. Vendors ended up with incompatible extensible-agent environments.
tldr.mechanism: AgentX splits an agent into one master agent that speaks SNMP and zero or more subagents that hold the management data. Subagents open sessions, register regions of the MIB, and the master agent dispatches AgentX PDUs to the right subagent.
tldr.outcome: A standard protocol lets independently developed master agents and subagents interoperate, while managers see an ordinary monolithic agent. This RFC obsoletes RFC 2257 and is a Draft Standard.

today: RFC 2741 is a Draft Standard published in January 2000 and obsoletes RFC 2257. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Extensible Agents Needed a Standard
sections.content:
New MIB modules are defined all the time, by IETF working groups and by enterprises. A managed device is therefore often a collection of components installed separately, and each component provides the instrumentation for the managed objects of the MIB modules it implements. The SNMP framework does not describe how the set of managed objects supported by an agent may change dynamically.

Many vendors built extensible agents to cope: a master agent on the standard transport address, a set of subagents with the management instrumentation, a private protocol between them, and tools to build subagents. Without a standard, a vendor might have to support several different subagent environments, and configuring subagents and master agents on one node could be cumbersome. AgentX is the standard protocol meant to fix both problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer is built from lots of parts that each know about their own stuff. Everyone used a different way for the parts to talk to the helper, which was a mess, so this RFC picks one way.

sections.title: Master Agents and Subagents
sections.content:
In the AgentX framework an agent consists of a single master agent and zero or more subagents. The master agent sends and receives SNMP messages in the agent role but typically has little or no direct access to management information. Subagents are shielded from SNMP messages but have access to the management information. They talk to each other using AgentX messages. The RFC stresses that AgentX is not SNMP, even though some messages look similar.

The master agent accepts session requests and registrations of MIB regions, applies MIB views and access control, and forwards notifications for subagents. A subagent opens sessions, registers regions, instantiates managed objects, performs management operations on variables and initiates notifications.

The design splits the work: the master agent is described as MIB ignorant and SNMP omniscient, and the subagent as SNMP ignorant and MIB omniscient for the variables it instantiates. Managers cannot tell the difference. An extensible agent behaves exactly like a monolithic agent with the same instrumentation, which is what separates AgentX from SNMP proxy agents.

Non-goals include subagent-to-subagent communication and subagent access to MIB variables through the master agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk knows how to talk to customers but not what is in the warehouse. The warehouse workers know their shelves but never talk to customers. Customers just see one shop.

sections.title: The AgentX PDU Header
sections.content:
Unlike SNMP, AgentX PDUs are not BER encoded. They are a contiguous byte stream aligned to 32-bit boundaries so that processors can read integers directly. Every PDU starts with a fixed 20-octet header: h.version (1 for this memo), h.type, h.flags, a reserved byte, then h.sessionID, h.transactionID, h.packetID and h.payload_length.

The flags are a bitmask: INSTANCE_REGISTRATION, NEW_INDEX, ANY_INDEX, NON_DEFAULT_CONTEXT and NETWORK_BYTE_ORDER. The last one says whether all multi-byte integers in the PDU, including the rest of the header, are big endian (set) or little endian (clear), so subagents can use their native byte order.

The master agent assigns the session ID in its response to the open request. The transaction ID ties together all AgentX PDUs that come from one SNMP management request, and it is not the SNMP request-id. The packet ID is chosen by the sender, and a response must echo the packet ID of the PDU it answers. The payload length excludes the 20-byte header and is always 0 or a multiple of 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Every AgentX message starts with the same label on the front: what kind of message it is, which conversation it belongs to, and how long it is.

sections.title: The Eighteen PDU Types
sections.content:
AgentX defines 18 PDU types. Types 1 to 4 and 12 to 17 are administrative PDUs. They open and close sessions, register and unregister MIB regions, send notifications, check liveness, allocate and release table indexes, and add or remove agent capabilities. Types 5 to 11 are used for SNMP request processing: Get, GetNext, GetBulk and the TestSet, CommitSet, UndoSet and CleanupSet steps of a Set.

A subagent starts with an agentx-Open-PDU, which carries a default timeout in seconds, an object identifier naming the subagent and a description. It then sends an agentx-Register-PDU for each region of the MIB naming tree it wants to support. The registration carries a priority from 1 to 255 (127 is the default) and may carry a range of one sub-identifier, so a conceptual row can be registered with a single PDU. An optional context can be included when the NON_DEFAULT_CONTEXT flag is set.

Every request is answered with an agentx-Response-PDU. It carries res.sysUpTime, res.error and res.index. Administrative errors are numbered from 256, such as duplicateRegistration (263). Compared with RFC 2257, the Notify and Close PDUs now generate a response and three error codes were added: parseFailed (266), requestDenied (267) and processingError (268).
sections.plainLanguage: There is a short list of message types, like "hello", "I handle this part", "what is the value" and "goodbye". Every question gets an answer message back.

sections.title: Registration and Dispatching
sections.content:
Because subagents register independently, the master agent may hold duplicate or overlapping regions. It picks one authoritative region by two rules: first the registration whose subtree has the most sub-identifiers (the most specific), then, if still tied, the one with the smaller r.priority. The value returned in the SNMP response must always come from the authoritative region. Subagents with no special knowledge should register with the default priority of 127.

When an SNMP request arrives, the master agent finds the region for each variable binding. If no region contains the name, the binding gets noSuchObject for a Get. The master agent may send one AgentX PDU with all bindings for a subagent or several PDUs with one each, except that for a Set all bindings for a session go in a single agentx-TestSet-PDU. All PDUs for one SNMP request carry the same transaction ID.

The timeout used for a region is the one given at registration if non-zero, else the session default if non-zero, else the master agent's own default. Index allocation is a master agent service that lets subagents that do not know each other share a conceptual table.

The RFC says the registry and dispatching algorithm is meant to be simple and deterministic: for any given region of the MIB there is a single authoritative subagent.
sections.plainLanguage: If two helpers both say they handle the same shelf, the front desk picks the one who knows the shelf best, or the one with the better rank. Then the answer always comes from one helper.

sections.title: Set Transactions and Session States
sections.content:
A Set is done in phases so that changes can be rolled back. A subagent that receives an agentx-TestSet-PDU checks whether all variable bindings are acceptable. If so it is ready to commit, otherwise the test failed. A agentx-CommitSet-PDU then performs the change, and an agentx-UndoSet-PDU reverses a commit. An agentx-CleanupSet-PDU ends the transaction.

The RFC lists three possible PDU sequences for a subagent: TestSet, CommitSet, CleanupSet; or TestSet, CommitSet, UndoSet; or TestSet followed directly by CleanupSet. If the session is lost, the subagent rolls back or undoes as needed and the transaction is done.

The RFC also gives state tables from the master agent's point of view for transport connections (no transport, or transport connected) and for sessions (no session, or session established). An Open-PDU on an established transport creates a session, and a Close-PDU ends it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like trying on a jacket before buying it. First check it fits, then buy it, and if something goes wrong you can give it back.

sections.title: Transport Mappings
sections.content:
The same PDU formats, encodings and procedures are used on every transport. The RFC defines two mappings.

Over TCP, the master agent accepts connections on well-known port 705. Several AgentX sessions may share one TCP connection, and the peers map each h.sessionID to a connection. Entities must not interleave the bytes of different PDUs, and a receiver must expect TCP to deliver byte sequences that do not line up with PDU boundaries.

Over UNIX-domain sockets, the master agent creates a well-known stream socket endpoint called /var/agentx/master. This suits setups that want to be sure subagents run on the same node as the master agent, or where sockets are faster than TCP or UDP, especially with heavy network I/O.
sections.plainLanguage: The helpers can talk to the front desk over the network, or through a private door when they are in the same building. The messages are the same either way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The master agent is assumed to authenticate SNMP requests and control access to management data, independently of the subagent. AgentX itself defines no way to authorize or refuse a session, and no access control on which subtrees a subagent may register. The RFC warns that a malicious subagent could register a sensitive subtree, see modification requests for it, or give clever answers that lead a management station to do something harmful.

No SNMP security information, such as community names, is passed from the master agent to the subagent. Controlling who may connect has to happen at a lower layer. With a local transport on the same host, the operating system can authorize the connection. With a network transport there is no inherent security, and TLS, SSL or IPsec SHOULD be used. The RFC RECOMMENDS that subagents always run on the same host as the master agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has no lock of its own on the door to the back room. So you should only let trusted helpers in, ideally ones working in the same building.

fields.name: h.sessionID
fields.desc: Identifies the session between subagent and master agent.

fields.name: h.transactionID
fields.desc: Identifies the SNMP request an AgentX PDU belongs to.

fields.name: h.packetID
fields.desc: Chosen by the sender; echoed in a response.

fields.name: h.payload_length
fields.desc: Octets after the header; 0 or a multiple of 4.
